name: TB-500

track.title: Lab & animal
track.line: Mouse, rat, horse and cell studies; few on TB-500

track.title: Pilot in people
track.line: One 3-patient case report, mixed with other drugs

track.title: FDA approval
track.line: Not approved; HHS compounding discretion, Oct 2026

what.text: TB-500 is a common name, not an official drug name. FDA describes it as a synthetic chain of seven amino acids, Ac-Leu-Lys-Lys-Thr-Glu-Thr-Gln (Ac-LKKTETQ), with an acetyl group on the first one. It copies amino acids 17 to 23 of thymosin beta-4, a 43-amino-acid protein found in many cells and body fluids. Its molecular weight is about 889 daltons.

src.label: FDA briefing document on TB-500, PCAC meeting July 2026

what.text: TB-500 and thymosin beta-4 are not the same substance. FDA notes that many websites use the two names as if they were. FDA has also found different salts and related molecules sold under the same name TB-500.

src.label: FDA briefing document on TB-500, PCAC meeting July 2026

what.text: According to FDA’s review, the seven-amino-acid fragment was first made from thymosin beta-4 in a 2003 study. A veterinary product called TB-500 appeared in 2011 and was marketed in horse and greyhound racing. Doping laboratories confirmed that its main ingredient is the acetylated fragment.

src.label: FDA briefing document on TB-500, PCAC meeting July 2026
Esposito S, et al. Drug Test Anal 2012
Ho EN, et al. J Chromatogr A 2012

what.text: How it acts, according to animal and cell studies:

items.text: Its sequence contains the part of thymosin beta-4 that binds actin, a protein that shapes cells and helps them move. Researchers have proposed that TB-500 binds actin the same way. FDA says it is not known whether this explains any of its reported effects.

src.label: FDA briefing document on TB-500, PCAC meeting July 2026

items.text: In horses given one injection under the skin, TB-500 reached the blood within about 1 to 2 hours and was broken down into shorter fragments. It could no longer be measured after 6 to 10 hours.

src.label: FDA briefing document on TB-500, PCAC meeting July 2026
Ho EN, et al. J Chromatogr A 2012

items.text: In a 2024 lab test on skin cells (fibroblasts), TB-500 itself did not close scratch wounds. One of its breakdown fragments, Ac-LKKTE, did, by a small amount.

src.label: Rahaman KA, et al. J Chromatogr B 2024

what.text: None of these mechanisms has been measured in people.
Adonis Clinical does not carry TB-500 today.

research.text: No clinical trial of TB-500 has published results. FDA’s 2026 review found no study in which TB-500 was given to people. Since then, one case report has described three dental patients who got TB-500 mixed with other drugs. The rest of the evidence is in animals and cells.
Each study is listed below exactly as it was run.

research.title: Nerve injury after dental surgery, 2026 (USA)

facts.v: uncontrolled case report inside a narrative review. No control group, no placebo.
3 adults (aged 38, 48 and 85) with numbness or altered feeling in the jaw and lip after implant or extraction surgery
weekly injections into the gum near the nerve of a mix of TB-500, BPC-157 and ARA-290, plus dexamethasone (a steroid) and a local anesthetic
4 weeks of treatment; follow-up time varied
size of the numb area and sensory recovery, as recorded by the clinicians

research.found: All three had less numbness by the end of follow-up, and no side effects were reported. The authors say this kind of injury often recovers on its own and that the effect of any one ingredient cannot be separated.

src.label: Froum S, et al. Front Oral Health 2026

research.text: The 2021 Florida knee pain chart review described on the BPC-157 page gave 4 of its 16 patients BPC-157 combined with “thymosin-beta-4 (TB4).” The paper does not say whether this was TB-500 or the full protein. Three of the four reported improvement by phone; there was no control group and no validated pain scale.

src.label: Lee E, Padgett B. Altern Ther Health Med 2021

research.text: ClinicalTrials.gov has one record naming TB-500 (NCT07487363, a Phase 1/2 study in adults with stable heart disease, listed as recruiting in China). The record’s own summary calls it “a fictional study” and “an example” record, so it is not counted here as a trial.

src.label: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT07487363

research.text: Studies of the full protein, thymosin beta-4 (not TB-500)

The full 43-amino-acid protein has been tested in people. These results do not apply to TB-500: FDA notes the two are different substances, and adding the acetyl group can change how a peptide behaves.

src.label: FDA briefing document on TB-500, PCAC meeting July 2026

items.text: randomized, placebo-controlled. 4 groups of 10 healthy volunteers got a single IV dose, then daily doses for 14 days. Side effects were infrequent and mild or moderate; there were no serious adverse events.

src.label: Ruff D, et al. Ann N Y Acad Sci 2010

items.text: randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled Phase 2. 9 patients used thymosin beta-4 eye drops (RGN-259) or a placebo drop for 28 days, with 28 more days of follow-up. Eye discomfort and corneal staining improved more than on placebo at several time points.

src.label: Sosne G, et al. Cornea 2015

items.text: randomized, double-masked, placebo-controlled Phase 3 with 18 patients. After 4 weeks, the eye surface defect healed fully in 6 of 10 on the drops and 1 of 8 on placebo; this main result was not statistically significant (p = 0.0656). No significant adverse effects were seen. Three authors work for the company developing the drops or its parent company.

src.label: Sosne G, et al. Int J Mol Sci 2022

research.title: Skin wounds in aged mice, 2003

facts.v: animal study. The fragment tested was LKKTETQ without the acetyl group, so not TB-500 itself.
26-month-old (aged) mice with small punch wounds on the back
the fragment, full thymosin beta-4 or a blank solution, put on the wounds
wound closure and collagen under the microscope

research.found: Both the fragment and the full protein increased wound closure and collagen compared with the blank solution. FDA notes there was no dose-response testing and the result may not carry over to TB-500.

src.label: Philp D, et al. Wound Repair Regen 2003
FDA briefing document on TB-500, PCAC meeting July 2026

research.meta: South Korea · 2024 · Cell and rat study
research.title: TB-500 breakdown and skin-cell wounds, 2024

facts.v: lab study in human serum and liver and kidney enzyme preparations; urine from rats given TB-500; scratch-wound test in skin cells
what TB-500 breaks down into, and whether TB-500 and its fragments close scratch wounds in cells

research.found: TB-500 was broken down into shorter fragments in all systems. TB-500 itself did not close scratch wounds; only the fragment Ac-LKKTE did. No fragment harmed the cells.

src.label: Rahaman KA, et al. J Chromatogr B 2024

research.title: Doping test in horses, 2012

facts.v: doping-control study. Horses were given one injection of a veterinary TB-500 product.
TB-500 and its breakdown products in blood and urine

research.found: TB-500 and several breakdown fragments were found in blood and urine. The study looked only at detection, not at any effect on healing.

src.label: Ho EN, et al. J Chromatogr A 2012

research.title: Achilles tendon repair in rats, 2026

facts.v: randomized animal study, 4 groups: no treatment, BPC-157, TB-500, or both
32 male rats after surgical cutting and repair of the Achilles tendon
daily injections into the abdominal cavity for 4 weeks
tendon strength (load to failure) and tissue scores under the microscope

research.found: The TB-500 group had stronger tendons and better tissue scores than untreated rats at 4 weeks. Combining it with BPC-157 added nothing. The authors call it exploratory.

src.label: Biçer O, et al. Jt Dis Relat Surg 2026

research.text: FDA found no animal toxicity studies of TB-500 at all: no single-dose, repeat-dose, DNA-damage, reproduction or cancer studies. Animal results have not been confirmed in people.

src.label: FDA briefing document on TB-500, PCAC meeting July 2026

items.text: FDA’s scientists, in a review dated May 15, 2026 for the July meeting, recommended against adding TB-500 (free base or acetate) to the list of substances pharmacies may compound. They cited unclear chemical identity, no known history of use in compounding, no human effectiveness data, no human safety data and a possible risk of immune reactions to injected peptides.

src.label: FDA briefing document on TB-500, PCAC meeting July 2026

items.text: FDA’s advisory committee voted on TB-500 on July 23, 2026: 8 in favor of adding it to the compounding list, 6 against and 1 abstaining, in both forms, as reported by Healio from the July 23–24, 2026 meeting. FDA has not posted the official vote record.

us.text: Not FDA-approved for any use. Since October 30, 2026, HHS has said it will not take enforcement action against licensed pharmacies and physicians that compound TB-500 acetate for injection under the skin or into muscle, under set conditions. That is enforcement discretion, not approval. As of October 31, 2026.

items.text: none. FDA’s 2026 review says TB-500 is not part of any FDA-approved drug and has no official drug monograph.

src.label: FDA briefing document on TB-500, PCAC meeting July 2026

items.text: a pharmacy nominated TB-500 for wound healing, as a 3 mg/mL injection under the skin or into muscle. The nomination was later withdrawn. FDA reviewed it anyway and, in May 2026, recommended against adding it to the 503A bulks list.

src.label: FDA briefing document on TB-500, PCAC meeting July 2026

items.text: FDA’s page of substances that may pose significant safety risks lists “thymosin beta-4, fragment (LKKTETQ), also known as TB-500” among nominations that were withdrawn. FDA says it has found no human exposure data and lacks key safety information.

src.label: FDA, bulk drug substances that may present significant safety risks (Category 2 page)

items.text: HHS announced an enforcement discretion policy on October 28, 2026, published in the Federal Register on October 30, 2026 (Docket HHS-OASH-2026-0496). It names TB-500 acetate, for injection under the skin or into muscle. HHS says it does not intend to take enforcement action against state-licensed pharmacies, federal facilities or licensed physicians that compound it when every condition is met. As of October 31, 2026.

src.label: HHS notice, Federal Register 2026-22192 (Docket HHS-OASH-2026-0496), signed by Secretary Kennedy, filed Oct 28, 2026
BakerHostetler summary of the HHS policy (a law firm's summary, used because HHS's own policy appendix could not be opened)

items.text: a licensed pharmacist or physician compounds it; the bulk substance matches the listed peptide and route; it comes from an FDA-registered maker that follows good manufacturing practice, with a valid certificate of analysis; there is a valid patient-specific prescription; the product contains only one active ingredient from the list; serious adverse events and quality problems are reported to FDA's MedWatch and state authorities; the label says "This is a compounded drug product. Not for resale."; oral forms have documented adequate bioavailability; the only device packaged with it is an FDA-cleared syringe; and all other section 503A requirements are met.

src.label: BakerHostetler summary of the HHS policy (a law firm's summary, used because HHS's own policy appendix could not be opened)

items.text: The policy does not make it FDA approved. It does not cover blends with other active ingredients, other routes or forms, outsourcing facilities (section 503B), or products sold as research chemicals or dietary supplements. It is interim and not binding: HHS may revise or withdraw it, in whole or in part, if safety signals or product-quality problems appear.

after.title: Sport
after.text: TB-500 is prohibited at all times under class S2.3 (growth factors and growth factor modulators) of the 2026 Prohibited List, which names “thymosin-β4 and its derivatives, e.g. TB-500.” Class S2 substances are not “specified substances.” WADA’s own copy of the list could not be opened for this page; the text was read in the Finnish anti-doping agency’s published version, which states that WADA’s English version is the official one. The 2027 list was not checked.

src.label: 2026 Prohibited List (WADA list), as published by the Finnish Center for Integrity in Sports

side.text: Almost nothing is known about TB-500’s side effects in people. FDA found no human safety studies and no animal toxicity studies. The few reports that exist are listed below.

items.text: FDA’s drug reporting system had no reports for TB-500 through March 26, 2025. FDA’s food and supplement complaint system had two reports about a “blended TB-500 and BPC-157” product, without safety details.

src.label: FDA briefing document on TB-500, PCAC meeting July 2026

items.text: in one FDA report, a 40-year-old woman injecting a “research purposes only” blend twice a day developed widespread skin darkening and darkened gums. It happened again when she restarted, and stopped when she quit. FDA could not tell which peptide caused it.

src.label: FDA briefing document on BPC-157, PCAC meeting July 2026

items.text: the three dental patients given TB-500 in a mix with other drugs had no side effects reported.

src.label: Froum S, et al. Front Oral Health 2026

items.text: FDA says injected peptides like TB-500 may carry a significant risk of immune reactions, made worse by clumping (aggregation) and impurities. Reactions can range from harmless antibodies to life-threatening ones.

src.label: FDA briefing document on TB-500, PCAC meeting July 2026

items.text: a representative supplier certificate for TB-500 that FDA reviewed did not test for impurities, bacterial toxins or clumping.

surprises: TB-500 is widely sold as “thymosin beta-4,” but FDA says it is a different substance: a seven-amino-acid fragment of the 43-amino-acid protein. Human trials of the full protein do not apply to it.

TB-500 is marketed for wound and tissue healing, yet the only lab test of TB-500 itself that FDA found showed no wound-closing effect in skin cells; only one of its breakdown fragments had a small effect.
FDA found no published study in which TB-500 was given to people, and no animal toxicity studies of any kind.

The only ClinicalTrials.gov record naming TB-500 (NCT07487363) describes itself as “a fictional study” and “an example” record. Its sponsor, Hudson Biotech, also sponsors the BPC-157 hamstring trial NCT07437547 cited on the BPC-157 page.
